verses.text: So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him. "Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women," he commanded.
"Go at once to Paddan-aram, to the house of your mother's father Bethuel, and take a wife from among the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother.
May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you may become a company of peoples.
And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants, so that you may possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham."
So Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, who was the mother of Jacob and Esau.
Now Esau learned that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife there, commanding him, "Do not marry a Canaanite woman,"
and that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and gone to Paddan-aram.
And seeing that his father Isaac disapproved of the Canaanite women,
Esau went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael, in addition to the wives he already had.
Meanwhile Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran.
On reaching a certain place, he spent the night there because the sun had set. And taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head and lay down to sleep.
And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God's angels were going up and down the ladder.
And there at the top the LORD was standing and saying, "I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie.
Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and east and north and south. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring.
Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."
When Jacob woke up, he thought, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it."
And he was afraid and said, "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!"
Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it,
and he called that place Bethel, though previously the city had been named Luz.
Then Jacob made a vow, saying, "If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey, and if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear,
so that I may return safely to my father's house, then the LORD will be my God.
And this stone I have set up as a pillar will be God's house, and of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth."

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Isaac’s sons, Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:19 to 36:43)
context.audience: Israel, named for Jacob, learning how God kept His promise through a flawed and struggling family
context.setting: Isaac blesses Jacob again, this time knowing who he is, and sends him to Paddan-aram to marry one of Laban’s daughters, praying that “the blessing of Abraham” would pass to him (vv.1-5). Esau, seeing that his parents dislike his Canaanite wives, marries a daughter of Ishmael as well (vv.6-9). Jacob leaves Beersheba alone. At sunset he stops, puts a stone under his head and sleeps (vv.10-11). He dreams of “a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven,” with God’s angels going up and down it, and the LORD standing above (vv.12-13). God gives him Abraham’s promise, the land, descendants “like the dust of the earth,” and blessing for “all the families of the earth” (vv.13-14), and adds a promise for the road: “I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land” (v.15). Jacob wakes: “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it” (v.16). He sets up the stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, names the place Bethel, house of God, and vows that if God brings him back, “the LORD will be my God” and he will give a tenth (vv.18-22).
context.custom: The Hebrew sullam, used only here, may mean a stairway or ramp rather than a ladder with rungs. Many scholars compare the stepped temple towers of Mesopotamia, whose stairs led up to a shrine for the god: here the stairway is God’s own, and He comes down to a fugitive sleeping on the ground. Standing stones (matsevot) marked holy places across Canaan; Jacob’s pillar marks where God spoke. Bethel became one of Israel’s chief places of worship, and later a center of Jeroboam’s golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-29).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 29 brings Jacob to a well near Haran, where he meets Rachel and starts working for Laban.
context.timelineBible: Jesus tells Nathanael, “you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51): Jesus Himself is the stairway between heaven and earth. Hosea remembers that God “found him at Bethel and spoke with him there” (Hosea 12:4). Jacob’s tenth echoes Abraham’s gift to Melchizedek (Genesis 14:20).

translation.meaning: A ladder or stairway, from a root meaning to heap up, used only here in the Bible.
A gate: the city gate where elders met and business was done. Jacob calls Bethel “the gate of heaven,” the way in to God’s presence.
A standing stone set up as a memorial or marker. Later law forbade pillars used in Canaanite worship (Deuteronomy 16:22).

gospelParallels.note: Angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
I will never leave you nor forsake you.
I am with you always, to the end of the age.

otBackground.note: Jacob returns to Bethel and God renews the promise.
He found him at Bethel and spoke with him there.
The LORD will watch over your coming and going.

overview.summary: On the run from Esau, Jacob sleeps at Bethel and dreams of a stairway to heaven; God gives him Abraham’s promise and pledges to go with him and bring him back.
overview.settingLine: Bethel, on the road north from Beersheba.

history.t: Mesopotamian temple towers had stairways up to a shrine.
Later a great sanctuary of the northern kingdom.

customs.t: A pillar marked a holy place or a promise.
A tithe was given to a god or a king.

archaeology.t: The village of Beitin north of Jerusalem is usually taken as Bethel.
Standing stones have been found at shrines such as Gezer and Arad.

overview.discussion: Jacob found God in a place he never expected (v.16). Where might God be present in my life right now without my noticing?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

historicalImage.caption: Jacob’s Dream, by Jusepe de Ribera (1639, Prado, Madrid). Ribera paints Jacob asleep in the open with only a faint golden light above him; the ladder is barely there, the dream is all in his face (Genesis 28:12).
